name: Whiskey Sour

ingredients.note: for a silky foam on top. Served raw: leave it out if you are pregnant, elderly or unwell

steps.text: Add the bourbon, lemon juice and syrup to a shaker. Add the egg white if you are using it.
Fill the shaker with ice and shake hard.
Strain into a short glass over fresh ice.

tools.name: Shaker
tools.alternative: A jam jar with a tight lid

whyItWorks: This is the basic sour: a strong spirit, sour lemon and sweet syrup in balance, so no single one stands out. Bourbon brings vanilla and oak. Once you can taste how the three parts fit, you can make most drinks in this family.

name: Daiquiri

steps.text: Add the rum, lime juice and syrup to a shaker.
Fill the shaker with ice and shake hard.
Strain into a chilled stemmed glass with no ice.

tools.name: Shaker
tools.alternative: A jam jar with a tight lid

whyItWorks: Three ingredients and nowhere to hide. Rum is the strong part, lime the sour and syrup the sweet. If it tastes too sharp, add a little syrup; if too sweet, a little lime. That adjustment is the main skill in mixing.

name: Margarita

ingredients.note: a pinch, for the rim of the glass

steps.text: For a salt rim, rub a cut lime around the edge of the glass and dip it in salt.
Add the tequila, orange liqueur and lime juice to a shaker.
Fill the shaker with ice and shake hard.
Strain into the glass over fresh ice.

tools.name: Shaker
tools.alternative: A jam jar with a tight lid

whyItWorks: A sour where the sweet part is a liqueur instead of syrup. Orange liqueur sweetens the drink and adds its own flavour and strength. Salt on the rim makes the lime taste brighter and softens any bitterness.

name: Gimlet

steps.text: Add the gin, lime juice and syrup to a shaker.
Fill the shaker with ice and shake hard.
Strain into a chilled stemmed glass with no ice.

tools.name: Shaker
tools.alternative: A jam jar with a tight lid

whyItWorks: The same shape as a Daiquiri with gin in place of rum. Compare the two and you can taste what the spirit alone contributes: here, juniper and citrus peel in place of sugar cane.

name: Sidecar

steps.text: Add the brandy, orange liqueur and lemon juice to a shaker.
Fill the shaker with ice and shake hard.
Strain into a chilled stemmed glass with no ice.

tools.name: Shaker
tools.alternative: A jam jar with a tight lid

whyItWorks: Built like a Margarita, with brandy and lemon in place of tequila and lime. The orange liqueur is the only sweetener, so the drink is quite dry. Brandy gives it a warm, dried-fruit depth.

name: Cosmopolitan

steps.text: Add the vodka, orange liqueur, cranberry juice and lime juice to a shaker.
Fill the shaker with ice and shake hard.
Strain into a chilled V-shaped glass with no ice.

tools.name: Shaker
tools.alternative: A jam jar with a tight lid

whyItWorks: Vodka adds strength but little taste, so the flavour comes from tart cranberry, lime and sweet orange liqueur. It shows how a neutral spirit lets fruit take the lead.

name: Amaretto Sour

ingredients.note: for a silky foam on top. Served raw: leave it out if you are pregnant, elderly or unwell

steps.text: Add the amaretto and lemon juice to a shaker. Add the egg white if you are using it.
Fill the shaker with ice and shake hard.
Strain into a short glass over fresh ice.

tools.name: Shaker
tools.alternative: A jam jar with a tight lid

whyItWorks: Amaretto is already very sweet, so it plays both the strong and the sweet part and needs no syrup. Lemon does all the balancing. It is lower in alcohol than most sours and a gentle place to start.

name: Bee's Knees

steps.text: Add the gin, lemon juice and honey syrup to a shaker.
Fill the shaker with ice and shake hard.
Strain into a chilled stemmed glass with no ice.

tools.name: Shaker
tools.alternative: A jam jar with a tight lid

whyItWorks: A gin sour sweetened with honey instead of sugar. Honey adds a floral flavour of its own, which suits the herbs in gin. Changing the sweetener is one of the easiest ways to change a drink.

name: Gin and Tonic

steps.text: Fill a tall glass to the top with ice.
Pour in the gin, then the tonic. Add a squeeze of lime if you like.

whyItWorks: One part spirit to three parts mixer is the usual highball ratio. Bitter tonic sharpens the pine-like juniper in gin. Plenty of ice keeps it cold and fizzy for longer, because a full glass of ice melts slowly.

name: Whisky Highball

steps.text: Fill a tall glass to the top with ice.
Pour in the whisky, then the soda water.

whyItWorks: Soda water adds no flavour, so this is whisky made longer and lighter. The bubbles carry the aroma up, which makes it a good way to get to know a bottle you usually drink neat.

name: Cuba Libre

steps.text: Fill a tall glass to the top with ice.
Add the rum and lime juice, then top with cola.

whyItWorks: A rum and cola with lime. The small amount of lime is what makes it a proper drink: its sourness cuts the sweetness of the cola and lets the rum come through.

name: Moscow Mule

steps.text: Fill a mug or tall glass with ice.
Add the vodka and lime juice, then top with ginger beer.

whyItWorks: Vodka supplies the strength and spicy ginger beer supplies the flavour. Lime ties the two together. It is traditionally served in a copper mug, but any glass works.

name: Dark and Stormy

steps.text: Fill a tall glass to the top with ice.
Pour in the ginger beer, then slowly pour the rum on top so it floats. Add a squeeze of lime if you like.

whyItWorks: The same idea as a Moscow Mule with dark rum in place of vodka. Because the rum has plenty of its own flavour, toffee and spice meet the heat of the ginger. Comparing the two shows how much the base spirit matters.

name: Paloma

steps.text: Fill a tall glass to the top with ice.
Add the tequila, lime juice and a pinch of salt, then top with grapefruit soda.

whyItWorks: Grapefruit is sour and slightly bitter, which suits the earthy taste of tequila. A pinch of salt softens the bitterness. It is as easy as a rum and cola and more refreshing.

name: No-Alcohol Mule

steps.text: Fill a mug or tall glass with ice.
Add the lime juice and top with ginger beer. Garnish with mint if you like.

whyItWorks: A Moscow Mule without the vodka. Because vodka adds almost no flavour, very little is lost: ginger and lime already carry the drink.

name: Lemon, Lime and Bitters

steps.text: Shake the bitters into a tall glass and swirl to coat the inside.
Fill the glass with ice, add the lime juice and top with the soda.

whyItWorks: A few dashes of bitters add spice and a touch of bitterness to a sweet soft drink, the way seasoning changes a dish. The bitters contain alcohol, but so little is used that the drink is under 1%.

name: Tom Collins

steps.text: Fill a tall glass with ice.
Add the gin, lemon juice and syrup and stir briefly.
Top with soda water and give one gentle stir.

whyItWorks: A gin sour made long with soda water. The strong, sour and sweet balance is the same; the soda makes it lighter and more refreshing, like a grown-up lemonade.

name: Mojito

steps.text: Put the mint, syrup and lime juice in a tall glass and press gently.
Add the rum and fill the glass with ice.
Top with soda water and stir gently from the bottom to lift the mint.

tools.name: Muddler (a blunt stick for pressing)
tools.alternative: The end of a wooden spoon

whyItWorks: A Daiquiri with mint and soda added. Pressing the mint gently releases its oils; crushing it makes it bitter. The soda lengthens the drink so it can be sipped slowly.

name: Gin Fizz

ingredients.note: for a foamy head. Served raw: leave it out if you are pregnant, elderly or unwell

steps.text: Add the gin, lemon juice and syrup to a shaker. Add the egg white if you are using it.
Fill the shaker with ice and shake hard.
Strain into a tall glass with no ice.
Top slowly with soda water so a foam rises.

tools.name: Shaker
tools.alternative: A jam jar with a tight lid

whyItWorks: Almost the same ingredients as a Tom Collins, but shaken and served without ice. Shaking adds air, and the soda lifts it into a foamy head. It shows how technique changes a drink even when the recipe barely does.

name: Virgin Mojito

steps.text: Put the mint, syrup and lime juice in a tall glass and press gently.
Fill the glass with ice, top with soda water and stir gently.

tools.name: Muddler (a blunt stick for pressing)
tools.alternative: The end of a wooden spoon

whyItWorks: A Mojito without the rum. Mint, lime and sugar are strong enough flavours to stand on their own, with a little more of each to fill the gap.

name: Shirley Temple

steps.text: Fill a tall glass with ice.
Add the grenadine and lime juice, then top with ginger ale.

whyItWorks: A classic drink with no alcohol. Sweet pomegranate syrup and gentle ginger are balanced by a little lime, the same sweet-against-sour idea as a cocktail.

name: Old Fashioned

ingredients.note: a strip of peel, to garnish

steps.text: Add the syrup and bitters to a short glass.
Add the bourbon and a few large ice cubes, then stir.
Squeeze the orange peel over the glass to release its oils, then drop it in.

whyItWorks: Whiskey with just enough sugar to soften it and bitters to season it. The spirit stays the star, which makes this the closest cocktail to drinking it neat. It is a good way to compare bottles you already own.

name: Manhattan

steps.text: Add the whiskey, vermouth and bitters to a mixing glass and fill it with ice.
Stir until very cold.
Strain into a chilled stemmed glass with no ice.

whyItWorks: Two parts whiskey to one part sweet vermouth. Vermouth plays the role that sugar plays in an Old Fashioned, and brings herbs and dark fruit as well. It is stirred, not shaken, so it stays clear and smooth.

name: Negroni

ingredients.note: a slice or strip of peel, to garnish

steps.text: Add the gin, Campari and vermouth to a short glass and fill it with ice.
Stir until very cold.
Garnish with the orange.

whyItWorks: Equal parts strong, bitter and sweet, which makes it easy to remember. Gin gives the strength, Campari the bitterness and vermouth the sweetness. It tastes bitter at first; many people grow to love it.

name: Dry Martini

steps.text: Add the gin and vermouth to a mixing glass and fill it with ice.
Stir until very cold.
Strain into a chilled V-shaped glass with no ice.

whyItWorks: Nearly all gin, softened by a little dry vermouth and by the water from stirring with ice. That small amount of dilution is essential: it opens up the flavour and takes off the burn. Serve it as cold as you can.

name: Boulevardier

ingredients.note: a strip of peel, to garnish

steps.text: Add the bourbon, Campari and vermouth to a short glass and fill it with ice.
Stir until very cold.
Garnish with the orange peel.

whyItWorks: A Negroni with bourbon in place of gin. The sweeter, rounder whiskey softens the bitterness of the Campari, so this is an easier first step into bitter drinks if you already like bourbon.

name: Rusty Nail

steps.text: Add the Scotch and Drambuie to a short glass and fill it with ice.
Stir until cold.

whyItWorks: Two ingredients. Drambuie is itself made from Scotch and honey, so it sweetens the whisky without changing its character. Use less Drambuie for a drier drink.

name: Aperol Spritz

steps.text: Fill a large wine glass with ice.
Pour in the sparkling wine, then the Aperol, then the soda water, and give one gentle stir.
Garnish with a slice of orange.

whyItWorks: Three parts sparkling wine, two parts Aperol, one part soda. The wine brings bubbles and acidity, the Aperol a gentle bitter orange flavour, and the soda keeps it light. It is lighter than most cocktails and hard to get wrong.

name: Americano

steps.text: Fill a tall glass with ice.
Add the Campari and vermouth, then top with soda water and give one gentle stir.
Garnish with a slice of orange.

whyItWorks: A Negroni with soda water in place of gin. You get the same bitter and sweet flavours in a much lighter drink, which makes it a gentle way to find out whether you like Campari.

name: French 75

steps.text: Add the gin, lemon juice and syrup to a shaker.
Fill the shaker with ice and shake hard.
Strain into a tall, narrow glass.
Top slowly with sparkling wine.

tools.name: Shaker
tools.alternative: A jam jar with a tight lid

whyItWorks: A small gin sour topped with sparkling wine instead of soda. The wine adds bubbles, acidity and extra strength, so it is livelier and stronger than it tastes.

name: Mimosa

steps.text: Pour chilled orange juice into a tall, narrow glass.
Top slowly with chilled sparkling wine. Do not stir, or it will lose its bubbles.

whyItWorks: Equal parts sparkling wine and orange juice. The juice softens the dry wine and the bubbles keep it light. Both should be well chilled, because no ice is used.

name: Bellini

steps.text: Spoon the peach purée into a tall, narrow glass.
Top slowly with chilled sparkling wine, stirring gently as you pour so it does not foam over.

whyItWorks: Two parts sparkling wine to one part peach. Soft, sweet fruit rounds off the acidity of the wine. It works with other ripe fruit too, which makes it a good drink to experiment with.

name: Kir Royale

steps.text: Pour the blackcurrant liqueur into a tall, narrow glass.
Top slowly with chilled sparkling wine.

whyItWorks: A spoonful of blackcurrant liqueur in a glass of sparkling wine. The liqueur adds sweetness, colour and fruit, and shows how a very small amount of a strong flavour can change a drink.

name: Piña Colada

steps.text: Add the rum, pineapple juice and cream of coconut to a blender with a large handful of ice. Add the lime juice if you are using it.
Blend until smooth.
Pour into a tall glass.

tools.name: Blender
tools.alternative: A shaker; shake hard with ice for a thinner drink

whyItWorks: Rum, pineapple and coconut: sweet, tangy and creamy together. The pineapple supplies the acidity that keeps the coconut from being too rich. A little lime sharpens it further.

name: Mai Tai

steps.text: Add the rum, orange liqueur, almond syrup and lime juice to a shaker.
Fill the shaker with ice and shake hard.
Strain into a short glass over fresh ice.

tools.name: Shaker
tools.alternative: A jam jar with a tight lid

whyItWorks: A rum sour with two sweeteners: orange liqueur and almond syrup. The almond gives the drink its nutty, rounded taste. Despite its reputation it contains no fruit juice except lime.

name: Virgin Piña Colada

steps.text: Add the pineapple juice, cream of coconut and lime juice to a blender with a large handful of ice.
Blend until smooth.
Pour into a tall glass.

tools.name: Blender
tools.alternative: A shaker; shake hard with ice for a thinner drink

whyItWorks: A Piña Colada without the rum. Pineapple and coconut already carry the flavour, and the lime keeps it from being too sweet.

name: White Russian

steps.text: Fill a short glass with ice.
Add the vodka and coffee liqueur and stir briefly.
Pour the cream slowly over the top so it floats.

whyItWorks: Coffee liqueur gives the flavour and sweetness, vodka the strength and cream the richness. It tastes like a sweet iced coffee, so the alcohol is easy to miss.

name: Espresso Martini

steps.text: Add the vodka, coffee liqueur and cooled coffee to a shaker. Add the syrup if you are using it.
Fill the shaker with ice and shake very hard to build a foam.
Strain into a chilled V-shaped glass with no ice.

tools.name: Shaker
tools.alternative: A jam jar with a tight lid

whyItWorks: Real coffee adds bitterness and aroma that the liqueur alone cannot. Shaking hard whips the natural oils in the coffee into a creamy foam on top, with no cream involved.

name: Irish Coffee

steps.text: Warm a mug or heatproof glass with hot water, then empty it.
Add the whiskey, syrup and hot coffee and stir.
Whisk the cream lightly so it thickens but still pours, then pour it gently over the back of a spoon so it floats.

whyItWorks: A hot drink. Sugar is not only for sweetness here: it makes the coffee dense enough for the cream to float. You drink the hot, sweet coffee through the cool cream.

name: Brandy Alexander

steps.text: Add the brandy, chocolate liqueur and cream to a shaker.
Fill the shaker with ice and shake hard.
Strain into a chilled stemmed glass with no ice.

tools.name: Shaker
tools.alternative: A jam jar with a tight lid

whyItWorks: Brandy, chocolate and cream: a dessert in a glass. The liqueur sweetens it, the cream makes it smooth, and the brandy adds warmth so it is not just sweet.

name: Singapore Sling

ingredients.note: a herbal liqueur in the original; the drink still works without it

steps.text: Add the gin, cherry liqueur and orange liqueur to a shaker. Add the Bénédictine if you are using it.
Add the pineapple juice, lime juice, grenadine and a dash of bitters.
Fill the shaker with ice and shake hard. The pineapple juice will froth.
Strain into a tall glass filled with fresh ice.

tools.name: Shaker
tools.alternative: A jam jar with a tight lid

whyItWorks: Singapore's best-known cocktail, first mixed at the Raffles Hotel in the early 1900s. It has a long list of bottles, but the idea is simple: a small measure of gin in a lot of pineapple juice, with cherry liqueur and grenadine for sweetness and colour and lime to keep it fresh. Shaking pineapple juice gives the foamy top.

name: Calamansi Sparkler

steps.text: Add the gin, calamansi juice and syrup to a shaker.
Fill the shaker with ice and shake hard.
Strain into a tall, narrow glass.
Top slowly with sparkling wine.

tools.name: Shaker
tools.alternative: A jam jar with a tight lid

whyItWorks: The calamansi lime juice sold at every hawker centre, turned into a cocktail. Calamansi is sharper and more fragrant than ordinary lime, so it gets as much syrup as juice. It is built the same way as a French 75, which shows how changing one citrus fruit changes the whole drink.

name: Milo Nightcap

ingredients.note: a barspoon is about a teaspoon, so this is 2 tablespoons

steps.text: Stir the Milo into the hot water in a cup until smooth, then let it cool for a minute.
Pour it into a shaker and add the brandy and milk.
Fill the shaker with ice and shake hard.
Strain into a short glass over fresh ice. For a Milo Dinosaur finish, sprinkle a little dry Milo on top.

tools.name: Shaker
tools.alternative: A jam jar with a tight lid

whyItWorks: Iced Milo with a measure of brandy. Milo is malty and chocolatey, and brandy has the same warm, dried-fruit sweetness, so the two blend instead of competing. Dissolving the powder in hot water first stops it clumping in cold milk.

name: Iced Kopi Cocktail

steps.text: Stir the condensed milk into the coffee while it is still warm, so it dissolves.
Pour it into a shaker and add the vodka.
Fill the shaker with ice and shake hard.
Strain into a short glass over fresh ice.

tools.name: Shaker
tools.alternative: A jam jar with a tight lid

whyItWorks: Kopi, the strong coffee-shop coffee sweetened with condensed milk, served iced with vodka. Condensed milk does two jobs at once: it sweetens the drink and makes it creamy. Vodka adds strength without getting in the way of the coffee.

name: Gula Melaka Old Fashioned

ingredients.note: a strip of peel, to garnish

steps.text: Add the palm sugar syrup and bitters to a short glass.
Add the rum and a few large ice cubes, then stir.
Squeeze the orange peel over the glass to release its oils, then drop it in.

whyItWorks: An Old Fashioned with rum in place of whiskey and gula Melaka, the palm sugar used in chendol and ondeh-ondeh, in place of white sugar. Palm sugar tastes of caramel and smoke, which suits the toffee notes in dark rum. It shows how the sweetener in a drink can carry flavour of its own.

name: Caipirinha

steps.text: Put the lime wedges and sugar in a short glass and press them firmly a few times.
Fill the glass with crushed or cracked ice and pour in the cachaça.
Stir well, lifting from the bottom, so the sugar dissolves.

tools.name: Muddler (a blunt stick for pressing)
tools.alternative: The end of a wooden spoon

whyItWorks: Brazil's national cocktail, made in the glass. Pressing whole lime wedges with sugar draws out both the juice and the oil in the peel, which gives a fuller lime flavour than juice alone. The sugar is the sweet part, the lime the sour and the cachaça the strong.

name: Mint Julep

steps.text: Put the mint, sugar and water in a short glass or metal cup and press gently.
Fill to the top with crushed ice and pour in the bourbon.
Stir until the outside of the glass frosts over.

tools.name: Muddler (a blunt stick for pressing)
tools.alternative: The end of a wooden spoon

whyItWorks: A Kentucky classic: bourbon, sugar and mint over a mound of crushed ice. Crushed ice melts quickly, so the drink starts strong and softens as you sip. Press the mint gently; tearing it releases bitterness.

name: Bloody Mary

ingredients.note: more if you like it hot
a pinch, or celery salt, with a grind of black pepper

steps.text: Add the vodka, tomato juice, lemon juice, Worcestershire sauce, hot sauce and a pinch of salt and pepper to a mixing glass with ice.
Stir gently until cold. Shaking would make tomato juice frothy.
Strain into a tall glass over fresh ice.

whyItWorks: A savoury cocktail, built like a seasoned soup. Tomato gives body, lemon keeps it bright, and Worcestershire, hot sauce and salt season it. Vodka adds strength without competing. Taste and adjust the seasoning, the way you would with food.

name: Black Russian

steps.text: Fill a short glass with ice and pour in the vodka and coffee liqueur.
Stir gently.

whyItWorks: Two ingredients: vodka for strength, coffee liqueur for flavour and sweetness. Float some cream on top and it becomes a White Russian, which shows how one extra layer changes a drink.

name: Godfather

steps.text: Fill a short glass with ice and pour in the Scotch and amaretto.
Stir gently.

whyItWorks: Equal parts Scotch and amaretto. The almond sweetness of the liqueur rounds off the whisky's smoky, malty edges. Swap the Scotch for brandy and you have a French Connection.

name: French Connection

steps.text: Fill a short glass with ice and pour in the brandy and amaretto.
Stir gently.

whyItWorks: A Godfather made with brandy instead of Scotch. Brandy's dried-fruit warmth and amaretto's almond flavour sit naturally together, so it tastes softer and sweeter than its whisky cousin.

name: Garibaldi

steps.text: Fill a tall glass with ice.
Pour in the Campari, then the orange juice, and stir.
Garnish with the orange.

whyItWorks: Campari and orange juice. The juice softens Campari's bitterness while its own orange notes match the liqueur's. Whisking or shaking the juice first makes it light and foamy, the way Italian bars serve it.

name: Tequila Sunrise

steps.text: Fill a tall glass with ice and pour in the tequila and orange juice.
Pour the grenadine slowly down the inside of the glass. It is heavier, so it sinks.
Do not stir. Garnish with the orange.

whyItWorks: The sunrise is the grenadine: heavier than the juice, it sinks to the bottom and leaves a red-to-orange fade. Stirring would spoil the look but not the taste, so it is up to you.

name: Screwdriver

steps.text: Fill a tall glass with ice and pour in the vodka and orange juice.
Stir gently.

whyItWorks: Vodka and orange juice, one part to two. Because vodka tastes of so little, the juice decides how good the drink is: freshly squeezed makes a real difference.

name: Horse's Neck

ingredients.note: if you like a little spice
a long spiral of peel, to garnish

steps.text: Hang a long spiral of lemon peel inside a tall glass and fill it with ice.
Pour in the brandy and ginger ale, add a dash of bitters if using, and stir gently.

whyItWorks: Brandy lengthened with gentle ginger ale. The long curl of lemon peel is the drink's trademark: it hangs over the rim like a horse's neck and scents every sip.

name: Pisco Sour

ingredients.note: for the foam. Served raw: leave it out if you are pregnant, elderly or unwell

steps.text: Add the pisco, lemon juice, syrup and egg white to a shaker.
Shake hard without ice first to whip the egg, then add ice and shake again.
Strain into a chilled stemmed glass and shake a few drops of bitters onto the foam.

tools.name: Shaker
tools.alternative: A jam jar with a tight lid

whyItWorks: The national drink of Peru, and the classic sour shape with a foamy top. Shaking first without ice whips the egg white into a thicker foam. The drops of bitters on top add aroma with every sip.

name: Sea Breeze

steps.text: Fill a tall glass with ice and pour in the vodka, cranberry juice and grapefruit juice.
Stir gently.

whyItWorks: Tart cranberry and a smaller amount of sharp, slightly bitter grapefruit. The grapefruit stops the cranberry tasting flat, much as bitters season a richer drink.

name: Long Island Iced Tea

steps.text: Fill a tall glass with ice.
Add the vodka, tequila, rum, gin, orange liqueur, lemon juice and syrup.
Top with cola, stir gently and garnish with the lemon.

whyItWorks: Five spirits in small measures, balanced by lemon and sugar and topped with a splash of cola for the colour of iced tea. It contains no tea, and it is much stronger than it tastes, so take it slowly.

name: Planter's Punch

ingredients.note: a strip of peel, to garnish

steps.text: Fill a short glass with ice.
Add the rum, lime juice, syrup and cold water and stir.
Squeeze the orange peel over the drink and drop it in.

whyItWorks: An old Jamaican recipe built on the rhyme 'one of sour, two of sweet, three of strong, four of weak': lime, sweetener, rum and water. The official recipe uses fresh sugar cane juice; syrup and a splash of water stand in for it here.

name: Sex on the Beach

steps.text: Fill a tall glass with ice and pour in the vodka, peach schnapps, orange juice and cranberry juice.
Stir gently and garnish with the orange.

whyItWorks: Sweet peach, juicy orange and tart cranberry, with vodka for strength. The cranberry is what keeps it from being sugary: it supplies the sour that balances the sweet.

name: Tommy's Margarita

steps.text: Add the tequila, lime juice and agave syrup to a shaker.
Fill the shaker with ice and shake hard.
Strain into a short glass over fresh ice.

tools.name: Shaker
tools.alternative: A jam jar with a tight lid

whyItWorks: A Margarita with agave syrup in place of orange liqueur. Agave syrup comes from the same plant as tequila, so it sweetens the drink while making the tequila taste more like itself.
